name: Bones of the hand
func: The 27 bones of the wrist and hand: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges. Together they make a flexible, strong framework for gripping, pinching and the fine movements of writing or surgery.

levels.kid:
Your hand is full of little bones, **27** in each hand! That's more than a quarter of all the bones in your body if you count both hands.

There are three groups:

In your **wrist** there are 8 tiny bones, shaped like pebbles, all snuggled together in two rows.

In your **palm** there are 5 long bones, one going to each finger and your thumb. You can feel them on the back of your hand.

In your **fingers** there are little bones called **phalanges**. Each finger has 3, but your thumb only has 2. Wiggle your fingers and count the bendy places!

With so many bones, your hands can do amazing things: draw, tie shoes, play piano and catch a ball.
levels.hs:
Each hand has **27 bones** in three groups:
- **8 carpal bones** in the wrist, in two rows. Proximal row (from thumb side): **scaphoid**, **lunate**, **triquetrum**, **pisiform**. Distal row: **trapezium**, **trapezoid**, **capitate**, **hamate**. A mnemonic: "She Looks Too Pretty; Try To Catch Her."
- **5 metacarpals** forming the palm, numbered 1 (thumb) to 5 (little finger). Each has a base, shaft and head; the heads are your **knuckles**.
- **14 phalanges**: each finger has a **proximal**, **middle** and **distal** phalanx; the thumb has only proximal and distal.

The proximal carpal row meets the **radius** to form the **wrist joint**. The carpals form an arch whose front is bridged by a strong ligament, the **flexor retinaculum**, creating the **carpal tunnel**, which carries the finger flexor tendons and the **median nerve** into the hand.

The thumb's **carpometacarpal joint** (between the trapezium and 1st metacarpal) is a **saddle joint**, which lets the thumb swing across the palm to touch the other fingertips. This movement, **opposition**, is a key reason human hands are so skilful.
levels.college:
**Carpal details**: the **scaphoid** bridges both rows and is the most commonly fractured carpal. The **pisiform** is a sesamoid bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon. The **hamate** has a **hook**, and the **capitate** is the largest carpal and the centre of wrist motion.

**Carpal tunnel** boundaries: the **flexor retinaculum** attaches to the **scaphoid tubercle** and **trapezium** laterally and to the **pisiform** and **hook of hamate** medially. Contents: the **median nerve** plus nine tendons (four FDS, four FDP, one flexor pollicis longus). The **ulnar nerve and artery** pass outside it, in **Guyon's canal**.

The **anatomical snuffbox** on the back of the thumb side of the wrist is bordered by the tendons of **extensor pollicis longus** (ulnar side) and **abductor pollicis longus + extensor pollicis brevis** (radial side). Its floor contains the **scaphoid** and trapezium, and the **radial artery** crosses it.

**Joints**: radiocarpal (condyloid), midcarpal, carpometacarpal (the thumb's is a saddle; the 4th and 5th are mobile, letting the palm cup), **metacarpophalangeal (MCP)** joints (condyloid, the knuckles), and **interphalangeal (PIP, DIP)** hinge joints, each with **collateral ligaments** and a thick **volar plate**.

The hand's **arches** (proximal and distal transverse, longitudinal) are kept by bone shape, ligaments and the intrinsic muscles (thenar, hypothenar, lumbricals, interossei).
levels.phd:
The hand skeleton arises from the **autopod** of the limb bud. Digit number and identity depend on **SHH** from the zone of polarising activity and on **Gli3** repression: Gli3 loss leads to **polydactyly**, while graded SHH exposure over time specifies digits from thumb to little finger. **5′ Hoxd and Hoxa genes** (Hoxd13, Hoxa13) are needed for autopod formation; HOXD13 mutations cause **synpolydactyly**. Digits separate when **BMP**-driven **apoptosis** removes interdigital tissue; failure gives **syndactyly**. Joints form at **Gdf5**-expressing interzones within continuous cartilage rods.

Carpal ossification follows a fairly predictable order, from the capitate and hamate in the first year to the **pisiform last** (around age 9–12), making hand X-rays a standard tool for estimating **bone age** (Greulich–Pyle atlas or Tanner–Whitehouse scoring), used in growth assessment.

Wrist kinematics is still debated. The **proximal carpal row** is an "**intercalated segment**" with no tendon attachments, moving in response to forces from the radius and distal row. The **dart-thrower's motion** (extension with radial deviation to flexion with ulnar deviation) occurs mainly at the midcarpal joint with little scaphoid and lunate motion, and may be the most functional plane of human wrist motion.

The human thumb is distinctive: a long thumb relative to the fingers, a broad trapezium–metacarpal saddle and strong flexor pollicis longus allow **forceful precision grip**. Studies of fossil hand bones (e.g. Australopithecus sediba, Homo naledi) and the trabecular patterns inside metacarpals are used to infer tool use in human ancestors.
levels.expert:
**Scaphoid fracture**: a fall on an outstretched hand with **anatomical snuffbox tenderness**, scaphoid tubercle tenderness or pain on thumb compression. Initial X-rays can look normal, so a suspected fracture is splinted and imaged with **MRI** or CT. The scaphoid's blood supply enters **distally** and flows backward (retrograde), so **proximal pole** fractures risk **non-union** and **avascular necrosis**. Displaced or proximal fractures often need **screw fixation**.

**Lunate/perilunate dislocations**: the lunate tips into the carpal tunnel (the "**spilled teacup**" sign on a lateral X-ray), compressing the median nerve; an emergency reduction is needed. **Scapholunate ligament** tears show a widened gap ("**Terry Thomas sign**").

**Metacarpal and phalanx injuries**: **boxer's fracture** of the 5th metacarpal neck after punching; **Bennett's fracture** (intra-articular base of the thumb metacarpal); **mallet finger** (extensor tendon avulsion at the DIP); **scaphoid**, **hook of hamate** (golf, baseball bat) fractures. Always check **rotational alignment**: when the fingers flex, they should all point toward the scaphoid; scissoring means malrotation.

**Carpal tunnel syndrome** (median nerve compression): night tingling in the thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger, **Tinel's** and **Phalen's** signs, and wasting of the **thenar eminence** in advanced cases. **Nerve conduction studies** confirm it. In general, treatment is splinting, steroid injection or surgical **carpal tunnel release**, one of the most common operations, often done by neurosurgeons and hand surgeons.

**Kienböck's disease** is avascular necrosis of the lunate, linked to negative ulnar variance.

keyPoints: Carpals: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform / trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate
Carpal tunnel carries the median nerve + 9 tendons
Snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise
Thumb CMC saddle joint allows opposition

test.q: How many phalanges are in one hand?
Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox suggests a fracture of which carpal bone?
test.explain: The scaphoid lies in the snuffbox floor and is the most commonly fractured carpal.

test.q: Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel?
test.explain: The ulnar nerve passes outside, through Guyon's canal.

test.q: Why do proximal pole scaphoid fractures often fail to heal?
choices: Blood supply enters distally and flows backward
test.explain: Retrograde blood supply makes the proximal pole prone to avascular necrosis.

test.q: A fracture of the 5th metacarpal neck after punching a wall is a ______ fracture.
test.explain: The knuckle drops and the fragment tilts toward the palm.
